lesson_title: The end of austerity: 'never had it so good'
claim: Wilson created a new Ministry of Technology and increased funding for higher education, overseen by a major expansion of universities following the Robbins Report of 1963 (which recommended expanding university places from around 130,000 to 350,000).
issue: The Robbins Report figures are significantly wrong. At the time of the report (1962/63), there were approximately 216,000–238,000 full-time students in higher education in Great Britain. The report recommended expanding places to approximately 558,000 by 1980/81 — not from 130,000 to 350,000. Both the baseline and the target in the lesson are substantially incorrect.
correction: The Robbins Report (1963) recommended expanding full-time higher education places from approximately 216,000 (at the time of the report) to approximately 558,000 by 1980/81.

lesson_title: Immigration: Windrush, race riots and Enoch Powell
claim: Out of the Notting Hill riots came, indirectly, the Notting Hill Carnival, founded in 1965 as a community-building response to the violence
issue: The year 1965 is incorrect. The first outdoor Notting Hill Carnival took place in August 1966, organised by Rhaune Laslett as a street festival for neighbourhood children. An indoor Caribbean Carnival was held from 1959 by Claudia Jones at St Pancras Town Hall. Neither date is 1965. Sources consistently give 1966 as the start of the outdoor street carnival that became the annual Notting Hill Carnival.
correction: The Notting Hill Carnival's outdoor street format began in 1966 (organised by Rhaune Laslett). An earlier indoor 'Caribbean Carnival' was established by Claudia Jones from 1959. The year 1965 is not supported by historical sources.

lesson_title: Changing attitudes to authority: the permissive society
claim: CND's first Aldermaston march took place at Easter 1958; it attracted an estimated 4,000 marchers from London to Aldermaston. By the early 1960s the march reversed direction (Aldermaston to London)
issue: The reversal of direction happened from 1959, not the 'early 1960s'. The 1958 march went from London to Aldermaston (organised by the Direct Action Committee, supported by CND). From 1959 onwards CND organised the annual march in the reverse direction — Aldermaston to London — to direct attention at Parliament. Saying 'early 1960s' implies it reversed around 1960–62 when it actually reversed in 1959.
correction: The march direction was reversed from 1959 (not the early 1960s). The 1958 march (London to Aldermaston) was the only one in that direction; all subsequent CND-organised marches ran Aldermaston to London from Easter 1959 onwards.

claim: The death toll for 1971 was 180; for 1972, the worst year of the Troubles, it rose to approximately 470 deaths.
issue: The 1971 figure of 180 is wrong. The CAIN/Wesley Johnston annual death statistics for the Troubles record 171 deaths in 1971, not 180. The 1972 figure of 'approximately 470' is broadly defensible (the actual figure is 476 by the same dataset), so the 1972 figure does not require correction.
correction: The death toll for 1971 was 171 (per the Malcolm Sutton index as recorded in the CAIN database). The 1972 figure of approximately 470 is broadly accurate (actual: 476).
